items.title: [pipecat-ai] Pipecat: Public exposure of Pipecat’s development runner can allow unauthenticated bot session creation
items.summary: Pipecat’s built-in development runner exposes endpoints that create bot sessions and, for the Daily transport, paid Daily rooms. These development endpoints intentionally do not authenticate callers.The runner binds to localhost by default and is designed exclusively for local development. It is not built or supported as a production server. Exploitation therefore requires an operator to deliberately make the development runner reachable from an untrusted network, such as by setting --host 0.0.0.0, publishing its port, or using a public tunnel without access controls.If exposed in this way, an unauthenticated caller may invoke endpoints including /start, /daily, and /daily-dialin-webhook. Depending on the endpoint and configuration, this can create a bot session or Daily room and may return a room URL and join token. Repeated requests may also consume local resources and third-party service quotas.The consequences of interacting with a launched bot depend on that bot’s configuration and connected tools. Access to external systems or sensitive information is not an inherent capability of the development runner and is therefore not included as a general impact.Pipecat 1.6.0 clarifies this security boundary in two ways:The development runner displays a prominent startup banner identifying it as a development tool.The documentation explicitly states that the runner must not be used as a production server or exposed directly to untrusted traffic.The local development documentation (https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/deployment/running-bots-locally) identifies the unauthenticated endpoints, lack of rate limiting, and risks of public exposure. The production deployment documentation (https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/deployment/running-bots-in-production) directs users to a production dispatcher or managed runtime and describes minimum protections for limited prototype use.ResolutionPipecat 1.6.0 documents and surfaces the intended security boundary of the development runner. The unauthenticated development behavior remains by design. Users must notexpose the runner directly to untrusted networks; production deployments require an authenticated dispatcher or managed runtime.Referenceshttps://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat/security/advisories/GHSA-hqm2-cfx2-2vghhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-102682https://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat/pull/5060https://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat/commit/acaac3e49f50968f3ffb645a42ecc48d71c4e723https://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat/releases/tag/v1.6.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hqm2-cfx2-2vgh

items.title: [jupyterlab] JupyterLab: Command link trust prompt in JupyterLab can trust a document other than the one clicked
items.summary: DescriptionA Markdown file or a notebook output can carry a button that runs a JupyterLab command. Since 4.5.7 the first click on such a button opens a prompt naming the command, with Cancel, Run Once and Trust. Choosing Trust runs the command and marks the document trusted, so its later buttons run without a prompt.Which document gets marked is decided when the user answers, not when they click. Both trust commands read whichever document is current at that moment: markdownviewer:trust uses tracker.currentWidget, and notebook:trust uses the equivalent lookup. If another document becomes current while the prompt is open, that document is the one marked trusted, and the one the user was looking at stays untrusted.Users are affected if all of the following are true:they run JupyterLab 4.5.7 through 4.6.3, or an application that bundles it such as Notebook 7.5+;they open a Markdown file or notebook from someone else and click a button in it;they answer Trust rather than Cancel or Run Once; anda second document becomes the current one while the prompt is open, for example through a workspace restoring at startup, an extension activating a widget, or a command that opens a fileImpactThe user loses control over which document they trusted. Every button in the document that was (incorrectly) marked as trusted runs from then on without a prompt, so if that document also came from an untrusted source, its buttons fire on a single click with no confirmation. That is the state the prompt was added to prevent, in GHSA-mqcg-5x36-vfcg.The command that ran had the user's consent, because the prompt named it and they pressed Trust. The document they were reading stays untrusted, so it prompts again on the next click.Notebooks are written to diskWhen the document marked is a notebook, the effect outlives the browser session. notebook:trust marks every cell trusted and then saves the file, which results in the server signing it, so the notebook stays trusted when it is next opened. The save also writes out any unsaved edits in that notebook. A second confirmation appears first, but it says only that a trusted notebook may execute hidden code, without naming the file, so it does not show the user which notebook is about to be trusted.A Markdown preview marked this way stays trusted only until it is closed. Nothing is written to disk.PatchesJupyterLab v4.6.4 and v4.5.11 contain the patch. The trust request now carries the document that was clicked, and the command is run only once that same document has been marked.Users of applications that depend on JupyterLab, such as Notebook v7+, should update jupyterlab package too.WorkaroundsGiven the high complexity of a potential exploit, we advise treating this as a defense in-depth and update at earliest opportunity, rather than apply the workarounds listed below. However, for users running in highly sensitive environments who are unable to upgrade the workarounds are included below. Turn off command linker, which removes the ability to execute frontend commands altogether:{  "@jupyterlab/apputils-extension:sanitizer": {    "allowCommandLinker": false  }}In such configuration the buttons in Markdown files and notebook outputs then do nothing when clicked. Documentation and extensions that use command links for navigation stop working, and the setting applies to every document, not only untrusted ones.If disabling that setting is not desirable and update is not possible, advise users to choose "Run Once" rather than "Trust". "Run Once" makes the command run but no document is marked, so nothing can be trusted in error.Referenceshttps://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/security/advisories/GHSA-jwrc-gm9j-263phttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-102832https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/commit/0fc18ab4ef67e431a8f6560e387193baf786c70ahttps://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/commit/b64bc88b8ca034cf158604a5cc48ca9170ea453bhttps://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/commit/f7e5f9803fdf2aaaa0e9bfb9cc73386a8cc5f0b2https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/releases/tag/v4.5.11https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/releases/tag/v4.6.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jwrc-gm9j-263p

items.title: [tinytag] tinytag: Infinite loop when parsing certain M4A files containing invalid atoms
items.summary: ImpactAn M4A file containing a sub-atom with a size of zero in the ---- atom makes the parser enter an infinite loop, resulting in a denial-of-service for programs reading such files with tinytag.PatchesThe issue has been fixed in tinytag 2.3.0, by reusing the primary atom parsing code path that contains appropriate size checks.WorkaroundsNo workarounds exist. Users must upgrade to tinytag 2.3.0.Referenceshttps://github.com/tinytag/tinytag/security/advisories/GHSA-24cc-9352-h2pghttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-104266https://github.com/tinytag/tinytag/pull/326https://github.com/tinytag/tinytag/commit/9ada221ba44990cb02cd9002d992186e037b515ehttps://github.com/tinytag/tinytag/releases/tag/2.3.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-24cc-9352-h2pg

items.title: [copyparty] copyparty FTP: upload outside defined volumes (limited path traversal)
items.summary: The FTP and FTPS server -- if enabled -- would allow uploading to any folder that the copyparty process had permission to write to.The FTP-server is default-disabled, and must be explicitly enabled in the config with global-option ftp or ftps to be affected. Additionally, SFTP was not affected at all; only FTP and FTPS.This was not a full read/write path-traversal; it had the following limitations:Only applied to uploads; it was not possible to read/download existing files in this manner.The output filename was not fully controllable; a randomized suffix would always be appended to the filename.Existing files could not be overwritten or appended to; only new files could be created.Filesystem-permissions would prevent writing to system folders, as copyparty surely does not run as root in most deployments.Copyparty itself will not execute arbitrary files as code by default, so this vulnerability could not be used to execute arbitrary code through copyparty.The main concern is the potential effect on other unrelated software which is running on the same system.The severity is assuming the worst case (SC:H/SI:H), that the same machine is running some unrelated software that will execute new arbitrarily-named files as code, and that the copyparty process has sufficient privileges to write files into the config-folder of that unrelated software.Referenceshttps://github.com/9001/copyparty/security/advisories/GHSA-phv8-wgjp-g4p9https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-104102https://github.com/9001/copyparty/commit/b331bb1c8c8cc306b91e4d94221969335a7a3e86https://github.com/9001/copyparty/releases/tag/v1.20.19https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-phv8-wgjp-g4p9

items.title: [unstructured] unstructured: Stored XSS via unescaped HTML generation
items.summary: SummaryWhen unstructured parses an untrusted document and outputs the result as HTML, malicious markup contained in the document (e.g. ) is left in the output HTML without escaping. When that output is displayed in a browser, the script embedded in the document executes in the viewer's browser.Detailspartition_html(html_parser_version="v2") (and the VLM partitioner) preserve the input document's element tags, attributes, and text into metadata.text_as_html, and elements_to_html() outputs that as an HTML document.The function that builds HTML on this path, to_html() in unstructured/documents/ontology.py, performs no escaping at all. items.title: [mcp] MCP Python SDK: Unbounded Session Accumulation in StreamableHTTP Transport Enables Resource Exhaustion
items.summary: SummaryIn affected versions, a Streamable HTTP server in stateful mode (the default) never reclaimed session state:sessions did not expire;a client DELETE ended the session but left its entry registered;a session whose first request was refused stayed registered with a running task.Each session also kept its parsed initialize parameters, and the number of sessions was unlimited. A client that could reach the endpoint could grow server memory without bound using ordinary short requests; only a restart reclaimed it.Am I affected?Yes, if you serve MCP over Streamable HTTP in stateful mode and clients you do not fully trust can reach the endpoint. Stateful mode is the default for:FastMCP (1.x)MCPServer and Server.streamable_http_app() (2.x)StreamableHTTPSessionManagerAffected versions: 1.8.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.Not affected:servers on 1.12.0 or later passing stateless_http=True (no sessions are kept)servers using only the stdio or SSE transportsAuthentication limits who can open sessions, not how many a token holder can open.FixUpgrade to mcp 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later. In those versions:a session with no request in flight for session_idle_timeout seconds (default 1800) is closed and its ID then answers 404; open streams and in-progress requests keep it alive;at most max_sessions sessions exist at once (default 10000); a request that would open another is answered 503;a session is discarded as soon as it ends, whether by DELETE, expiry, or a refused opening request.Both settings are keyword arguments on FastMCP(...) (1.x), MCPServer.run() / streamable_http_app() (2.x) and StreamableHTTPSessionManager; None disables them.This bounds retention rather than eliminating it: a live session still holds its initialize parameters (up to roughly twice the 4 MiB body limit), and an initialize with invalid parameters still opens a session that expires like any other. On a small host, lower session_idle_timeout, max_sessions and max_request_body_size to fit.If you cannot upgrade yet, pass stateless_http=True (1.12.0 or later) where you need no per-session state, or restrict who can reach the endpoint.Referenceshttps://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/security/advisories/GHSA-84m7-p3x7-pcfvhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-59951https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/pull/3395https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/pull/3426https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/commit/92120b4b0f50385af096592d7cee932fc1d994e7https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/commit/d2290ca3434731b68ea3e2270bc06a6e6575931bhttps://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/releases/tag/v1.30.0https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/releases/tag/v2.2.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-84m7-p3x7-pcfv

items.title: [borgbackup] borg extract might modify out-of-tree files when extracting maliciously crafted archives
items.summary: ImpactA maliciously crafted archive could contain a symlink (e.g. "evil" -> "/etc") followed by an item below it ("evil/passwd"), or an item whose path embeds ".." (e.g. "a/../../etc/passwd").When extracting such items, borg followed the symlink / resolved the "..", so it could delete or overwrite files outside the extraction directory.In a quite similar scenario, a crafted archive could contain a slave hardlink item with the hardlink source pointing outside the extraction directory.When extracting such an item, borg would hard-link the outside and the inside item.Note: that sounds bad, but it is no big issue in practice: to create such a malicious archive, the attacker would need repository access and (for encrypted or authenticated repos) also the borg key and passphrase.Affected: likely all borg releases before 1.4.5 (and also all borg 2.0.0 betas before b22).Patches1.4.x release series: fix released with 1.4.5. commits 3e9ed6d1ad6d3531b39c07b8ef3ecf41fce4437f and 141888f2fabcd57a300547c2aa63212cb213924d.1.2.x release series: no new releases any more, fix commits available on 1.2-maint branch: 0ac568e290518c3bbe781459978720dde7fab224 and d907f2cb57337041c4fa55ca4682895535e5076b2.0.0 betas: fix will be in 2.0.0b22, fix commits on master branch: 2d632531028b09da8ab5d1450f89bebcc205d640 and 4f37fdfed10b50559a0dd333b0d5581c642af329WorkaroundsFor encrypted or authenticated repositories, do not share borg key and passphrase with potential attackers.For all kinds of repositories, do not share repository access with potential attackers. Usually, the repository access is protected by means outside of borg; e.g. a ssh key for remote repositories or physical access to local storage media.ReferencesThis issue was first discovered by AI in a private code security review initiated by @ThomasWaldmann.A few days later, it was also independently reported to @ThomasWaldmann by:Michael Head (machin0r)Chinnapak Charoensiri [Github: Ziim-eiei].Referenceshttps://github.com/borgbackup/borg/security/advisories/GHSA-gfp8-w835-v44jhttps://github.com/borgbackup/borg/commit/0ac568e290518c3bbe781459978720dde7fab224https://github.com/borgbackup/borg/commit/141888f2fabcd57a300547c2aa63212cb213924dhttps://github.com/borgbackup/borg/commit/2d632531028b09da8ab5d1450f89bebcc205d640https://github.com/borgbackup/borg/commit/3e9ed6d1ad6d3531b39c07b8ef3ecf41fce4437fhttps://github.com/borgbackup/borg/commit/4f37fdfed10b50559a0dd333b0d5581c642af329https://github.com/borgbackup/borg/commit/d907f2cb57337041c4fa55ca4682895535e5076bhttps://github.com/borgbackup/borg/releases/tag/1.4.5https://github.com/borgbackup/borg/releases/tag/2.0.0b22https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gfp8-w835-v44j

items.title: [social-auth-core] Python Social Auth: Login CSRF in LINE backend (LineOAuth2) — missing OAuth state validation (incomplete fix of 5.0.0 campaign)
items.summary: ImpactApplications using the LINE Login backend are vulnerable to login CSRF / forced authentication. An attacker can start a LINE authorization flow for an account they control and trick a victim into visiting the callback URL with the attacker’s authorization code. Because the LINE backend did not validate the returned OAuth state, the application could accept the forged callback and log the victim in as the attacker-controlled LINE account.If account linking is enabled, the same flaw can allow an attacker to link their LINE identity to a victim’s existing authenticated account, creating a persistent unauthorized login path.Patcheshttps://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/pull/1829Workarounds  Only applications that enable the LINE backend are affected.CreditsThanks to Ta Duc Thien and Duc Anh Nguyen for reproting this via GitHub.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/security/advisories/GHSA-526j-582w-7fm9https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/pull/1829https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/commit/5b3b90d07ebccc1f5b076445b27ea35ec059764bhttps://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/releases/tag/5.0.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-526j-582w-7fm9
